papers.title: Split-RL: Local Conflict Resolution in Reinforcement Learning
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34799v1

summary.one_liner: Split-RL uses guidance labels to build gradient boosting trees that route conflicting reinforcement-learning feedback into separate state-space regions, evaluated on constrained and offline RL with mixed datasets.
summary.plain: Robots and other learning agents are often trained with feedback that pulls in opposite directions depending on the situation, such as going fast in open areas but carefully through tight gaps. This paper proposes Split-RL, which uses hints or rule-based labels to split the situations an agent can face into regions, so each conflicting goal is learned in its own region rather than blended together. The authors report that it met cost limits in their tests while keeping competitive rewards, and performed well in offline settings with mixed datasets.
summary.why: Conflicting objectives that apply only in certain places or moments are a common practical problem for learned controllers, and the paper offers a way to combine learned policies with existing rules. The text does not show how broadly the approach generalizes beyond the domains tested, so its wider significance is uncertain.
summary.background:
- Reinforcement learning: an agent learns a policy (a decision rule) by trying actions and receiving reward or penalty signals.
- Constrained RL: the agent must keep a secondary quantity, such as accumulated cost per episode, under a budget while maximizing reward.
- Offline RL: learning from a fixed log of past data rather than new interaction.
- Gradient boosting trees: an ensemble of decision trees built one after another, each correcting the errors of the previous ones; trees split the input space into regions.
- Neural networks share parameters across all inputs, so conflicting updates from different situations can interfere with each other.
- Gradient: the direction in which model parameters should change to reduce error; aggregating conflicting gradients can cancel useful information.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) policies are often trained by mixing contradictory feedback that is localized in space and time. For example, a robot may prioritize speed in open areas versus precision in tight gaps. We introduce Split-RL, a Gradient Boosting Trees (GBT) algorithm that uses guidance labels to locally isolate these conflicting signals. Standard neural networks (NNs) lack the structural mechanism to do this, as their parameters share feedback from all sources. While GBT provides the inductive bias to explicitly partition the state-space per objective, standard tree-fitting procedures aggregate contradictory gradient signals before they reach the leaves. Split-RL leverages this bias to integrate guidance labels into tree construction, routing these updates into disjoint state-space regions and preventing signal interference. Such labels can arise from heuristics, sensor-derived events, or existing rule-based systems, allowing Split-RL to incorporate rule-derived structure while retaining a learned policy. We theoretically show how early gradient aggregation loses objective-specific information and characterize when the Split-RL score isolates conflicting updates. We focus on constrained RL and offline RL with mixed datasets, each balancing two objectives that conflict locally. Across domains with spatial, rare-event, and temporal conflicts, Split-RL consistently outperforms existing methods by meeting the episodic cost budget while maintaining competitive rewards. In offline settings, Split-RL localizes the tradeoff between imitation and policy improvement, outperforming other methods and achieving near-expert performance across varying dataset sizes.

papers.title: Provably Efficient Concave Utility Reinforcement Learning with Linear Function Approximation
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34678v1

summary.one_liner: Proposes a model-based optimistic policy optimization framework (OCUPO) for concave utility RL in finite-horizon bilinear and linear MDPs, with on-policy and off-policy algorithms whose sample complexities are reported as Õ(ε^-4) and Õ(ε^-2) respectively, up to a projection error in the off-policy case.
summary.plain: Standard reinforcement learning trains an agent to maximize a sum of rewards. This paper studies a more general version, where the goal is a nonlinear function of how often the agent visits each situation and takes each action. The authors show how to estimate those visit patterns efficiently when the environment has a simple low-dimensional structure, and they give algorithms with provable sample-efficiency bounds.
summary.why:
The text gives theoretical sample-complexity bounds and says the off-policy version matches the epsilon-dependence of standard RL with linear function approximation, which suggests the general goal can be handled at little extra cost. It does not report experiments, so practical impact is untested; the connection to applications such as imitation learning and exploration is stated in the abstract as motivation only.</even>
<parameter name="background">- Reinforcement learning (RL): an agent learns by trying actions in an environment and receiving rewards.
- Occupancy measure: the long-run frequency with which an agent visits each state and takes each action.
- Concave utility RL (CURL): the goal is a concave (curved, diminishing-returns style) function of the occupancy measure, which covers imitation learning and maximum-entropy exploration.
- Markov decision process (MDP): a standard mathematical model of an environment with states, actions, and transitions.
- Linear and bilinear MDPs: environments whose transition behavior can be expressed with a small set of known features, making learning tractable.
- Function approximation: using a parameterized formula to generalize across many states instead of storing each one.
- Sample complexity: how many interactions with the environment are needed to reach a given accuracy ε; smaller exponents mean fewer samples.
- Off-policy learning: learning from data gathered by earlier versions of the policy rather than only the current one.

papers.abstract: Concave utility reinforcement learning (CURL) unifies a diverse range of problems, including standard reinforcement learning (RL), imitation learning, and maximum entropy exploration. Unlike standard RL, CURL generally requires estimating high-dimensional state-action occupancy measures. Consequently, existing methods for CURL either sidestep the exploration problem, are restricted to the tabular setting, or lack computationally efficient policy optimization. To address this, we study CURL in finite-horizon episodic bilinear MDPs, where the transition model admits a low-dimensional representation in known feature spaces. We use the bilinear structure to efficiently estimate occupancy measures via low-dimensional feature expectations, and propose a model-based optimistic concave utility policy optimization (OCUPO) framework. We first instantiate OCUPO in the on-policy setting, where each iteration uses independent trajectories to estimate the concave utility policy gradient, and prove an $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-4})$ sample complexity. To improve sample efficiency, we then instantiate OCUPO in the off-policy setting. We propose a novel backward feature regression subroutine that reuses trajectories collected by past policies to estimate the occupancy measure of the current policy. Under suitable technical assumptions on the policy class (satisfied, e.g., by log-linear policies with sufficiently expressive features), we prove that the resulting algorithm achieves an $\widetilde{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity, up to a controllable projection error. We further extend our framework to linear MDPs and show that the resulting off-policy algorithm retains the same sample complexity. In these settings, the dependence on $\epsilon$ matches that for standard RL with linear function approximation. Moreover, our algorithms do not rely on the integral oracle required by prior work.

papers.title: Provably Efficient Offline Discounted Reinforcement Learning under Recursive Entropic Risk
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34840v1

summary.background:
- Markov decision process (MDP): a model of sequential decisions where actions lead to probabilistic new states and rewards.
- Reinforcement learning (RL): learning a policy (a strategy for choosing actions) by trial and reward.
- Offline RL: learning only from a fixed, previously collected dataset, with no new interaction.
- Discount factor gamma: weights near-term rewards more than distant ones; the horizon is effectively about 1/(1-gamma) steps.
- Entropic risk measure: a way of scoring uncertain outcomes that penalizes (risk-averse, beta > 0) or rewards (risk-seeking, beta < 0) variability, applied recursively over time.
- Sample complexity: how much data is needed to reach a near-optimal policy with high probability (PAC-style bound).
- Lower confidence bound (LCB): a pessimistic estimate used to handle parts of the state space with little data.
summary.one_liner: This paper gives sample-complexity guarantees for offline, model-based reinforcement learning under a recursive entropic risk measure in discounted infinite-horizon MDPs, covering both risk-averse (beta > 0) and risk-seeking (beta < 0) settings, via an algorithm called ERM-VI-LCB.
summary.plain: This is about teaching a computer agent to make good decisions from a fixed log of past experience, while caring not just about average outcomes but also about how risky they are. The authors propose an algorithm and prove how much data it needs to reach a near-optimal policy. They also show that part of the data requirement, which grows exponentially with a risk-tuning parameter, cannot be avoided in the worst case.
summary.why: Risk-aware decision making matters wherever a bad tail outcome is costly, such as in finance, medicine, or robotics, and offline learning matters where live experimentation is expensive. The text claims these are the first rigorous sample-complexity guarantees for this combination, though I have not checked that claim against the wider literature.

papers.abstract: We study risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in finite discounted infinite-horizon Markov Decision Processes with recursive entropic risk measures (ERM), parameterized by $\beta\neq 0$. We consider both risk-averse ($\beta>0$) and risk-seeking ($\beta<0$) settings. We consider the offline RL setting, where the agent is provided with a fixed dataset and wishes to learn a near-optimal policy using this dataset. We introduce a model-based algorithm, called ERM Value Iteration Lower Confidence Bound (ERM-VI-LCB) and derive a PAC-type bound on its sample complexity. We also establish a corresponding lower bound, demonstrating that exponential dependence on $|\beta|/(1-\gamma)$ asserted by the upper bound is unavoidable in the worst case. The presented bounds provide the first rigorous sample complexity guarantees for offline RL under recursive ERM across both risk-averse and risk-seeking regimes.

papers.title: Effect-Driven Skill Abstractions for Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33229v1

summary.background:
- Reinforcement learning: an agent learns by trial and reward; here it learns from a fixed dataset of past experience (offline RL).
- Goal-conditioned RL: the agent is given a target state or goal to reach.
- Skill abstraction: short sequences of actions grouped into a reusable unit, so a planner picks among units instead of individual moves.
- Action chunks: fixed-length sequences of low-level actions treated as one unit.
- Quantization / discretization: mapping continuous values onto a finite set of codes (a "vocabulary").
- Low-level controller: a learned component that turns a chosen skill back into continuous actions.
- Baselines: established methods used for comparison.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes learning discrete skill vocabularies for offline, goal-conditioned RL by quantizing action chunks with an objective that predicts next states from the current state and action, so skills are distinguished by their effects.
summary.plain: Teaching a robot or simulated agent to plan in longer steps often means grouping small movements into reusable "skills." This paper proposes a way to build a small set of such skills by judging each one by what it does to the agent's surroundings, rather than by how well it reconstructs the original movements. The authors report that this approach, plugged into common offline learning methods, gave substantial and consistent gains on benchmark navigation and manipulation tasks compared with continuous-action baselines and reconstruction-based alternatives.
summary.why: Choosing among a finite set of skills, instead of outputting continuous motor commands, could make long-horizon planning easier to structure. The paper's central idea, that skills should be defined by the states they lead to, is a clear conceptual point, though the text alone does not show how well it generalizes beyond the benchmarks tested.

papers.abstract: We seek to learn discrete skill abstractions to facilitate long-horizon, goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning (RL) tasks. Recent approaches have shown success by quantizing actions via clustering or reconstruction. However, these objectives lead to skills that are not directly related to what the current state affords or what the goal requires. Instead, we argue that goal-directed skills should be driven by \emph{how they affect the state} of the agent. To realize this, we introduce a novel quantization method for action chunks that optimizes next-state predictions conditioned on the current state and action. This objective encourages skills to be distinguished by the future states they lead to, resulting in a vocabulary that spans diverse outcomes reachable from a given state. Our framework can easily be paired with common offline RL methods by replacing their continuous actor head with a discrete one that selects among the learned skills. We can execute these skills in the environment by converting them back to continuous actions using a trained low-level controller. Experiments on benchmark navigation and manipulation tasks largely show substantial and consistent improvements over both the continuous-actor baselines and reconstruction-based discretizations. Our project page can be found at: https://burcukilic.github.io/projects/effect-driven-skill-abstractions/.

papers.title: To Critic Or Not To Critic
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32013v1

summary.background:
- Reinforcement learning (RL): training by rewards from trial and error.
- Policy gradient: the direction in which to nudge a model so it earns more reward.
- Critic / value function: a learned estimate of expected future reward, used to judge actions.
- Advantage: how much better an action was than expected.
- Bias vs. variance: a noisy estimate (high variance) versus one that is systematically off (bias). Critics reduce noise but can introduce bias when they are wrong.
- Bootstrapping: updating estimates using other estimates, which can propagate errors.
- Batch size: how many examples are used per update; larger batches give less noisy gradients.
- PPO and GRPO: two popular RL algorithms; GRPO scores each attempt relative to its group, with no critic.
summary.one_liner: An empirical study of when a learned critic (PPO) beats critic-free group-based advantage estimation (GRPO) in RL, framed as a bias-variance tradeoff in gradient direction across batch sizes, horizons, and domains including LLM tasks.
summary.plain: Training AI systems with trial-and-error rewards often uses one of two methods: one trains a helper "critic" that estimates how good each step is, and the other skips the helper and compares a group of attempts instead. This paper asks when the helper is worth its cost. Across more than 1,200 training runs, the authors find that the helper-based method tends to win when batches of training data are small, while the simpler group method catches up as batches grow, and needs bigger batches on longer, harder tasks.
summary.why: Many recent language-model training results compare these two methods without a clear rule for which to use, so a set of conditions for the choice is useful to practitioners. The text reports the trends but does not show how far they generalize beyond the tasks tested.

papers.abstract: As large language models tackle longer and more complex tasks, understanding when a critic improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning (RL) becomes increasingly important. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) trains a critic to reduce variance and provide fine-grained credit assignment, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) drops the critic and avoids the bias of bootstrapping from the critic's value estimates. Although recent critic-based methods have reported strong performance relative to GRPO, it remains unclear when each approach is preferable. We argue that there is no universal answer; instead, the choice depends on several interacting factors, including batch size, critic reliance, and task complexity. We study the bias-variance tradeoff in terms of gradient direction, measuring how closely each method's gradient estimates align with the true policy gradient as batch size grows. Under a shared actor objective, we compare GRPO with PPO in control tasks, short-horizon math, and long-horizon terminal agents. Across more than 1,200 training runs, including 96 with LLMs, we find that PPO generally leads at small batch sizes, while GRPO often overtakes heavily bootstrapped PPO and reaches parity with lightly bootstrapped PPO at larger batches. At longer horizons and in more complex domains, GRPO needs larger batches to catch up to PPO's performance. Accounting for training compute, critics pay off at small budgets, but their returns diminish at larger budgets.

papers.title: Lazy Agents Answer Against Their Own Beliefs: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs Teaches Them to Act on What They Believe
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32884v1

summary.background:
- Reinforcement learning: training by rewarding actions that lead to good outcomes.
- Reward signal: the score the agent gets; an end-of-episode reward only scores the final answer.
- Posterior: the probability distribution over possible answers given the evidence seen so far.
- Vision-language model: an AI model that takes both images and text as input.
- GRPO and PPO: two common reinforcement learning training algorithms; the paper compares against them.
- Process reward from an LLM judge: a score on intermediate steps given by another language model.
- GPU-hours: a measure of computing cost.
- Laziness here means committing to an answer before the evidence supports it.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes RLVB, a reinforcement learning reward that uses the simulator's exact posterior over the answer to teach vision-language agents when to stop gathering evidence and commit, and introduces the Pro Worlds visual-puzzle benchmark.
summary.plain: AI agents solving multi-step tasks often give an answer too early, before they have seen enough evidence. The authors train agents with a reward that checks, during training only, whether the evidence so far already settles the answer, and rewards the agent for exploring when it does not and for answering when it does. They report gains over the base model on nine test settings, with some of the tests using tasks not seen in training.
summary.why: Premature guessing is a practical failure for agents that work through long tasks, and the paper's point that a final-answer-only reward cannot teach timing is a clear, testable claim. The approach's reliance on a simulator that can compute the exact answer probability during training limits where it applies, so its wider relevance is uncertain.

papers.abstract: AI agents working on long tasks often commit to an answer before they have enough evidence, a behavior called laziness. In our evaluations, they frequently commit even while their stated belief still names several possible answers. An outcome reward at the end of the episode scores only the final answer, so it cannot teach the agent when to commit, because a lucky guess receives the same reward as an answer backed by evidence. During training, however, the simulator can compute the exact posterior over the answer at every step and tell whether the evidence is already enough. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), which rewards the agent for taking further steps while this posterior still allows several answers and for committing once the evidence is sufficient. The reward needs no judge, critic or reward model, and it never reads the belief line the agent writes before each action. We also introduce Pro Worlds, a benchmark of visual puzzles where the agent views a large world through a small window. We evaluate three vision-language models on three benchmarks, two of which are never seen in training. RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average. Under the outcome reward, GRPO and PPO fall below the base model on average. RLVB also outperforms PPO with a process reward from an LLM judge by 9.3% on average while using 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of the episodes on the three benchmarks, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for the base model. Its accuracy gain therefore comes from answering more often at high levels of evidence. The belief line shows how the agent reaches this evidence: it acts on its own belief. It commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of the turns at which the evidence is insufficient and its line still names several answers, against 3 to 68% for the base model.

papers.title: Adopting AI Technologies without Traps: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30200v1

summary.background:
- Markov decision process (MDP): a standard way to model decisions over time, where an agent picks actions, the world moves to a new state, and the agent receives a reward.
- Reinforcement learning (RL): a method where an agent learns which choices lead to the best long-term reward through trial and feedback.
- Multi-agent RL (MARL): several learning agents interacting in the same environment, here both human and AI agents.
- State transition: a change in the situation (for example, a worker's skill level) caused by an action.
- Economic equilibrium: a stable point where no participant gains by changing behavior on their own.
- Skill erosion: losing a capability through disuse, such as when a task is always done by a machine.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes a general multi-agent Markov decision process (MARL) framework, covering human and AI agents, for finding long-term optimal strategies for adopting AI, and applies it to skill erosion from AI offloading, firm workforce structure, and labor/trading equilibria.
summary.plain: The paper asks how people and firms can adopt AI tools without falling into long-term traps, such as losing skills, losing jobs, or losing training opportunities. It builds a modeling framework in which human and AI agents make decisions over time, and negative effects appear as bad state changes or negative rewards. The authors apply this framework to three cases: skill erosion from handing tasks to AI, the best mix of human staff for a firm using AI, and the economic balance of trading and employment between humans and AI.
summary.why: Concerns about AI reducing human skills and jobs are widely discussed, and this paper offers a formal way to model those long-term effects using decision-making tools. The text is a framework description and does not show what the optimal strategies turn out to be in concrete numbers, so its practical value is not yet established from this excerpt alone.

papers.abstract: AI technologies and AI agents play increasingly important roles in human society, including in education, economics, and research. Adopting AI technologies can bring immediate, and sometimes tremendous, rewards such as through productivity boost, but they can also bring negative effects including but not limited to losses of job and training opportunities, and cognitive capability declines. Thus, it is important to investigate the optimal ways of adopting AI technologies without different traps. In this paper, we develop a general multi-agent Markov decision process (MDP) based reinforcement learning (RL or MARL) modeling framework for determining and analyzing optimal adoption of AI technologies. This framework can model the long-term dynamic effects of AI adoption, and lead to finding the optimal AI adoption strategies. In our modeling framework, the negative effects of AI adoption are modeled by undesirable state transitions or negative rewards in the MDPs. The proposed multi-agent RL MDPs incorporate both human agents and AI agents. The key idea of our models is that incorporating AI technologies may not only increase the immediate rewards for AI agents but also alter the states of the involved human and AI agents. In particular, we apply this framework to analyzing AI offloading leading to skill erosion, to analyzing optimal human resource structures for a firm adopting AI, and to analyzing the economic equilibria in the trading/employment among human and AI agents. Since the multi-agent MDP based RL technique is from control, machine learning and AI, this research is essentially using an AI technique to determine the optimal ways of adopting or co-existing with AI without traps.

papers.title: From Vanishing Gradients to Recursive Self-Improvement: Evaluating the Most Influential Papers in Large Language Model Evolution (1997-2026)
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29303v1

summary.background:
- Recurrent neural network (RNN): a model that reads text one word at a time and carries a running memory; it tends to lose early context.
- Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM): an RNN variant with gates that control what is kept, updated, or output.
- Word2Vec: a method that represents words as numerical vectors so that meaning relationships become arithmetic.
- Transformer and attention: an architecture where every word can look at every other word; powerful but costly as text grows.
- Scaling laws (Chinchilla): the finding that model size and training data should grow together.
- RLHF: training a model using human preference ratings to make it behave more helpfully and safely.
- Jailbreak: a crafted prompt that gets a model to ignore its safety training.
- Model collapse: quality degradation when models are trained on output generated by other models.
summary.one_liner: A review that walks through 22 influential publications on large language models (1997 to 2026), organized as a chronological cause-and-effect taxonomy, covering RNNs, LSTMs, Word2Vec, Transformers, scaling laws, RLHF, jailbreaks, and recent work on model collapse and self-improving agents.
summary.plain: This is a survey that tries to sort out which AI research results were real turning points and which were small refinements, by following one line of work from older neural networks through today's chatbots. It explains each step in everyday terms, such as a memory mechanism that decides what to keep, and then covers newer concerns like safety guardrails being easy to bypass and AI systems being trained on AI output. The text provided is a short abstract-style description, so it does not show the detailed evidence behind each claim.
summary.why: It offers a single narrative connecting early sequence models to current safety problems, which may help non-specialists see how the pieces relate. The abstract gives only the outline, though, so readers should check the cited papers themselves before relying on its judgments of which work mattered most.

papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Large Language Model (LLM) research makes it increasingly difficult to distinguish incremental refinements from true paradigm shifts. This review evaluates 22 of the most influential publications spanning nearly three decades (1997-2026), organized through a causal, chronologically anchored taxonomy centered on the author's birth year (1999). Beginning "before 1999" with how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) forgot earlier context (much like forgetting Chapter 1 by the time a reader reaches Chapter 9), we trace how Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks introduced a "bouncer" mechanism of forget, input, and output gates to selectively preserve long-term memory. We then examine how Word2Vec turned language into vector mathematics (king - male + female ~ queen), why sequential RNNs hit a parallelization wall, and how the Transformer's all-to-all attention weights launched the modern LLM era alongside a quadratic bottleneck. Next, we analyze why scaling parameters alone leaves capacity under-trained unless data scales equally (Chinchilla), how Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) left alignment superficial, and how that gap compounded into adversarial jailbreaks and single-direction refusal subspaces (J-space), where instructing a model not to think of a restricted concept surfaces it much like the human "red ball" paradox. Finally, we synthesize the current state of AI (2024-2026), encompassing recursive model collapse, autonomous reasoning-model jailbreak agents, machine-speed agentic intrusions, and closed-loop recursive self-improvement (AIDE^2).

papers.title: Testing for Coordination Failures in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27368v1

summary.background:
- Reinforcement learning: an AI learns by trying actions and receiving rewards.
- Multi-agent reinforcement learning: several agents learn at the same time, here aiming at one shared goal.
- Q-value: a learned estimate of the total future reward from taking an action in a given state.
- Coordination failure: agents' individual choices work against each other, so the team does badly.
- Test case selection: choosing which situations to run a system in, to find failures efficiently.
- Random testing and genetic-algorithm search: standard baseline methods for finding failures.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes DisQ, a test-case selection method that uses a "Q-value gap" (disagreement between agents' value estimates in a state) to find failure-revealing states when testing value-based cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning policies.
summary.plain: Teams of AI agents that learn to work together can behave unsafely in ways their reward signal does not capture, and those failures are hard to explain. This paper proposes a way to pick which situations to test by flagging states where the agents' estimates of future reward diverge beyond a set threshold. The authors report that, in most of four benchmark environments tested, this selection finds more failures than random testing or genetic-algorithm search methods borrowed from single-agent testing.
summary.why: Testing multi-agent systems for safety has received less attention than testing single agents, and the authors offer an explainable signal computable from one state without running the system. Its practical value beyond the four benchmarks evaluated is not established in the text.

papers.abstract: Deep parallel cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL)} trains multiple agents that all act at every time step to optimize a common objective. Like single-agent RL, CMARL can produce unsafe behaviors that violate implicit safety requirements not captured by the reward, and these behaviors are hard to explain. However, testing CMARL policies for safety has received less attention than the safety testing of single-agent RL policies. In this paper, we propose DisQ, a test case selection method that identifies failure-revealing states in value-based CMARL by exploiting a signal specific to trained Q-learning agents. The signal is the Q-value gap, an explainable metric that flags a state when the agents' estimates of the achievable return diverge by more than a calibrated threshold. DisQ selects such states for execution and skips those without a gap. Our experiments in four CMARL benchmark environments show that, in most of the evaluated configurations, DisQ improves failure detection over single-agent RL testing methods applied to CMARL, namely random testing and search-based testing with genetic algorithms. Our main contributions are the Q-value gap, an indicator of potential miscoordination computable from a single state without executing the system, and DisQ, a test case selection method that adapts existing single-agent testing methods to CMARL.

papers.title: Decision Models Are General-Purpose Process Reward Models
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27068v1

summary.background:
- Reinforcement learning (RL): training by trial and reward; here an AI language agent learns from task success or failure.
- Policy gradient: a family of RL update rules that make good actions more likely.
- Reward and credit assignment: deciding which steps in a long attempt deserve the credit or blame for the result.
- Process reward model (PRM): a scorer that rates intermediate steps, not just the final outcome.
- Advantage: how much better an action turned out than expected; used to scale the learning update.
- GRPO, PPO, GiGPO, HGPO, GraphGPO: named RL training methods for language agents; PPO uses a learned critic.
- ALFWorld and WebShop: simulated benchmarks for household tasks and online shopping.
- Zero-shot: used without task-specific training.
summary.one_liner: DM-PRM turns a general-purpose yes/no decision model into a zero-shot, step-level process reward that is added to the advantage in policy-gradient RL for language agents, evaluated on ALFWorld and WebShop.
summary.plain: Training AI agents with reinforcement learning usually gives one score at the end of a whole attempt, so the agent cannot tell which individual steps helped. This paper proposes asking a general yes/no question about each step, using a model's probability answer as a step-by-step score, without extra labels or training. The authors report that this improves the GRPO training method on two household and web-shopping task benchmarks, and that it helps other methods too.
summary.why: It offers a way to get per-step credit without hand-made step labels or a separately trained critic, which are costly to build. Whether this holds beyond the two benchmarks and one small model (Qwen2.5-1.5B) is not shown in the text, so its broader value remains to be tested.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) from verifiable outcomes gives a language agent one reward per episode: every step is credited alike, and nothing about the task is learned when all rollouts fail. The last mile, step-level credit, usually requires step labels, a learned critic, costly LLM judges or hand-written rules. We introduce DM-PRM, which turns a general-purpose decision model -- one answering yes/no questions with probabilities -- into a general-purpose process reward model (PRM), zero-shot: no step labels, no fine-tuning, no critic. DM-PRM asks one question per step and adds the standardised answers to the advantage. It plugs into any policy-gradient method; one model, with one question text per environment, serves household tasks, web shopping and multiple RL methods. With Qwen2.5-1.5B it lifts GRPO by over twenty points on ALFWorld and over ten on WebShop, overtakes GiGPO on ALFWorld and learns in far fewer iterations; it also improves GiGPO and GraphGPO on both benchmarks and reaches the highest success of our comparison, ahead of critic-based PPO and of state-of-the-art GiGPO, HGPO and GraphGPO. Its scores locate useful steps in failed rollouts, and trained agents drop idle actions and explore instead of circling. DM-PRM shows that step credit need not be learned: it can be asked for.

papers.title: Decision-Focused Reinforcement Learning for LLM Post-Training
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25597v1

summary.background:
- Large language model (LLM): a neural network trained on text that can also be used to output numbers or predictions.
- Post-training: extra training applied after a model's initial training, here to shape its predictions.
- Reinforcement learning (RL): training by giving a model a score (reward) for its outputs and adjusting it to earn higher scores.
- Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): training a model further on labeled examples, used here as a baseline.
- Optimization problem: choosing the best action under constraints, such as how much stock to order given predicted demand.
- Decision regret: the extra cost incurred because a decision was based on a prediction, compared with the best decision possible with perfect information.
- Knapsack problem: a classic problem of picking items to maximize value within a weight limit.
- Policy gradient: a standard RL method for adjusting a model's behavior using its reward signal.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes decision-focused reinforcement learning (DFRL), which post-trains LLMs to produce optimization parameters by rewarding them with negative downstream decision regret, and introduces two ways to cut the cost of exact reward evaluation.
summary.plain: Language models are often used to make forecasts, but a more accurate forecast does not always lead to a cheaper decision when that forecast feeds into an optimization problem, such as planning inventory. This paper trains a language model with reinforcement learning so that it is scored on the cost of the resulting decision rather than on how close its forecast is. On an inventory planning task using H&M transaction data and product descriptions, the authors report that their best setup, where the model reasons before predicting, cut regret by 31.4% relative to a supervised fine-tuning baseline and by 12.4% relative to the strongest conventional forecasting baseline they tested.
summary.why: It targets a real gap: forecasts judged only by accuracy can still lead to poor decisions, and training against decision cost directly addresses that. Its relevance beyond the tested problems (synthetic tasks, a knapsack task, and one inventory setting) is not established by the text, so the reach of the approach is still open.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as predictors across various tasks, benefiting from their ability to use information from unstructured context. However, when predictions serve as parameters of downstream optimization problems, higher prediction accuracy does not necessarily translate into lower decision costs. We propose decision-focused reinforcement learning (DFRL), a framework for post-training LLMs to predict optimization parameters using negative downstream decision regret as reward. DFRL trains LLM predictors to minimize the costs of the decisions induced by their predictions, without requiring downstream convexity or differentiability, and integrates readily into existing RL post-training frameworks. To address expensive reward evaluation, we develop two approaches. Heuristic warm-starting uses inexpensive approximate rewards during an initial phase before switching to refinement with exact rewards. Reward correction combines inexpensive estimates with randomized exact evaluations, preserving the expected policy gradient while reducing the expected number of exact solves per update. Experiments on three synthetic optimization problems demonstrate improvements over prediction-loss baselines, while a larger knapsack experiment shows faster early improvement under short training budgets. On inventory planning with H&M transactions and product descriptions, our best configuration, in which the LLM reasons before predicting, reduces regret by 31.4% relative to the SFT baseline and 12.4% relative to the strongest evaluated conventional forecasting baseline.

papers.title: Goal-Guided Reinforcement Learning via Fine-Tuning Vision-Language Models
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25742v1

summary.background:
- Reinforcement learning (RL): an agent learns by trying actions and getting rewards or penalties.
- Sparse rewards: rewards arrive rarely, so the agent struggles to learn what to do.
- Exploration: trying new things to discover useful situations.
- Craftax-Classic: a grid-based survival and crafting game used as a test environment for RL agents.
- Vision-language model (VLM): an AI model that takes both images and text as input.
- Fine-tuning: further training a pretrained model on a specific dataset.
- Direct Preference Optimization (DPO): training a model to prefer outputs that people or labels ranked higher, without a separate reward model.
- KL regularization: a penalty that keeps the trained model close to its original behavior.
- Distributionally robust reweighting: adjusting training weights so the model performs acceptably across uncertain or varied conditions.
summary.one_liner: The paper fine-tunes a vision-language model on a goal-preference dataset (CCGP-2M) from Craftax-Classic, using a new preference-optimization method (KLTDPO), so that it can propose exploration goals that guide a reinforcement learning agent.
summary.plain: Game-playing AI agents often struggle to explore because rewards are rare and tasks are long. This paper uses a model that understands both images and text to suggest high-level goals for the agent, after first training it on a dataset of which goals people or systems preferred in a Craftax-style game. The authors report that their approach collected diamonds earlier than the baselines they compared against and scored highest on score, reward, and most achievement success rates.
summary.why: It is a concrete attempt to make language-and-vision models useful for guiding exploration in sparse-reward games, rather than relying on hand-written prompts. The text reports results only on Craftax-Classic, so how well it transfers to other environments or real tasks is not shown here.

papers.abstract: Exploration remains a major challenge for reinforcement learning (RL) agents in Craftax-style environments due to sparse rewards and long horizons. Large language models (LLMs) can guide exploration by generating high-level goals, but methods using models without explicit task adaptation often rely on carefully designed prompts and may produce inconsistent or contextually inappropriate goals. We introduce CCGP-2M, a multimodal goal-preference dataset constructed from interaction trajectories in Craftax-Classic, and propose a vision-language model (VLM)-guided RL framework that learns environment-specific goal guidance from this dataset. The framework consists of two stages: offline VLM fine-tuning and online goal-guided RL. In the offline stage, we align the VLM with goal preferences using Kullback-Leibler Token-level Direct Preference Optimization (KLTDPO), which combines token-level KL regularization with distributionally robust reweighting. Experiments on Craftax-Classic show that our method collects diamonds earlier than state-of-the-art baselines, achieves the highest score and reward, and attains the highest success rates on most achievements.

papers.title: Replay, Don't Resample: Off-Policy Consolidation of Long-Horizon RL Experts
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24059v1

summary.background:
- Reinforcement learning (RL): training by trying actions and receiving rewards for good outcomes.
- Expert model: a version trained for one specific domain.
- Distillation: training a student model to imitate the output probabilities of one or more teacher models.
- On-policy vs. off-policy: on-policy learns from the model's own current attempts; off-policy learns from attempts generated by some other process, such as logged earlier runs.
- Rollout: one complete attempt at a task, recorded with its actions, probabilities and reward.
- Policy gradient: the update rule that nudges a model toward actions that led to higher reward.
- Clip range: a limit on how far each update can change the model, for stability.
- Long-horizon agentic task: a multi-step task where the model acts over many turns, such as searching or writing SQL queries.
summary.one_liner: MRPD consolidates several RL-trained domain experts into one student by replaying the experts' logged training rollouts, in the order the experts saw them, instead of sampling new data with on-policy multi-teacher distillation (MOPD).
summary.plain: Training AI models today often means first training separate "expert" versions, each good at one task, and then merging them into a single model. The usual merging step is expensive because it generates fresh practice attempts and has teachers score them again. This paper proposes reusing the record of what the experts already did during their own training, replaying it in the same order to train one combined model.
summary.why: The paper reports that the replay approach matches or beats the standard merging method at a fraction of its cost, on three multi-step tasks (reasoning, search and SQL). It also claims the order of the training records matters more than their size or reward values, which, if it holds up, would suggest those logs are better treated as a learning sequence than as a data pile; the text alone does not show how general this is.

papers.abstract: Frontier post-training follows a common recipe: train one expert per domain with reinforcement learning (RL), then consolidate the experts into one model via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Such consolidation is expensive: the student samples in every environment again, an expert scores every sampled token, and the student inherits the drift of the final experts. Yet we argue that the experts' RL runs have already produced what consolidation needs: rollouts with their sampling probabilities and rewards, in the order the experts learned from them. We propose multi-expert replay policy distillation (MRPD), which replays these training logs through the student in the experts' order. At each step, the policy gradient is recomputed on these scored trajectories, and the final experts' distributions are distilled at the logged prefixes. Following the experts' own trajectory reduces the training-inference mismatch and keeps the student within the clip range, so the replay is off-policy in origin but quasi-on-policy throughout consolidation. MRPD samples nothing and calls no environment or reward model: the trainer is the sole process, and consolidating the experts costs only about a seventh of the compute used to train them. On three long-horizon agentic domains (reasoning, search and SQL), MRPD yields the best student model, substantially outperforming online RL baselines, and surpassing MOPD from the same experts at a fraction of MOPD's cost. Our analysis on the same logs shows that the replayed trajectories carry most of the gain, and that both the policy gradient and the distillation term add to it. Most interestingly, the order of the logs matters more than their amount or rewards, suggesting that expert training logs are a curriculum, not a data mixture.

papers.title: Variance-Adaptive Upper Confidence Bounds for Multi-Armed Bandits with Kaplan--Meier Survival Estimation
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24988v1

summary.background:
- Multi-armed bandit: a setting where an algorithm repeatedly picks one of several options (arms) and learns their average payoff only from what it picks.
- Upper confidence bound (UCB): a rule that favours options whose payoff estimate could still be high given uncertainty.
- Right-censoring: the event of interest (e.g., death) has not been observed by the end of follow-up, so the record only says it happened after some time.
- Kaplan-Meier estimator: a standard method for estimating survival curves despite censored records.
- Greenwood's formula: a standard estimate of the variance (spread of uncertainty) of a Kaplan-Meier survival estimate.
- Empirical Bernstein bound: a confidence bound that uses the observed variance, so it can be tighter when outcomes are less variable.
- Regret: how much reward is lost compared with always picking the best option; logarithmic regret grows slowly with the number of rounds.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes KM-UCB, a variance-adaptive upper-confidence bandit policy for right-censored survival rewards, using a fixed-cohort empirical Bernstein bound built on Greenwood's variance formula and a Kaplan-Meier estimator, with a logarithmic regret claim under catch-up reporting.
summary.plain: The paper looks at choosing between several treatment options when the result for each is whether a patient survives to a set time, but some patients leave a study before that time, so their outcome is only partly known. The authors build a decision rule that adjusts how much it explores based on how uncertain each option's survival estimate is, and they test it in simulations and on replayed breast cancer trial data. The text describes both the method and its theoretical guarantee, and also mentions a separate paired-simulation check of a correction.
summary.why: Adaptive allocation of patients to treatments under censored outcomes is a practical problem in clinical trial design, so the work may matter there. How much it helps in real trials is not established by the text, which describes simulations and one retrospective replay.

papers.abstract: We study the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem in which the reward associated with each arm is the survival probability at a pre-specified time horizon, and the observed outcome is a right-censored time-to-event variable. Standard bandit algorithms face delayed and partial observations in this setting. Prior adaptations for the Kaplan--Meier (KM) estimator rely on Hoeffding-type bounds that ignore the inherent heteroscedasticity of continuous survival processes. To bridge this gap, we propose KM-UCB, a variance-adaptive policy that unites continuous-time survival analysis with discrete sequential decision-making. By leveraging martingale theory and continuous influence functions, we derive a fixed-cohort empirical Bernstein bound parameterized by Greenwood's variance formula. For realtime allocation, we retain the Greenwood index and use a survival bound from completed records to review the recommended arm. Under catch-up reporting, the policy has logarithmic expected regret with an arm-specific variance term in the exploration bound. We evaluate the original policy in a dual-layer delayed simulation and a retrospective replay of breast cancer trial data, and evaluate the correction in a separate paired simulation.

papers.title: Option-GRPO: Hierarchical RL Against AI Slop in Code Generation for Unseen SDKs
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23633v1

summary.background:
- Large language model (LLM): a neural network trained on text, including code, that generates new text or code.
- Reinforcement learning (RL): training by trial and error, where the model gets a reward signal for good outcomes.
- GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization): an RL method that scores several sampled answers against each other to decide which to reinforce.
- Pass@1: the fraction of tasks solved correctly on the first attempt.
- SDK (software development kit): a set of libraries and functions a programmer uses to build software for a platform.
- API call: a single request to a library function; fewer calls usually means more efficient code.
- Semi-Markov decision process: a decision model where actions can last multiple steps, used here for multi-step code-building options.
- Curriculum: training ordered from simpler to harder tasks.
summary.one_liner: Option-GRPO applies hierarchical reinforcement learning, using reusable code patterns extracted from SDK source code as options and a curriculum, to adapt a 32B code LLM to unseen SDKs while rewarding both functional correctness and concise, idiomatic code.
summary.plain: AI coding models often write code that works but is bloated, repetitive, and unidiomatic, and this gets worse for software libraries released after the model was trained. This paper proposes a training method that teaches a model a new library using only its source code, without hand-written examples or tests, by breaking the library into reusable building blocks and training step by step. The authors report that on 12 unseen libraries their method solved 61.4% of tasks on the first try and produced programs with about 35% fewer API calls than a standard baseline.
summary.why: Verbose, redundant generated code is a practical cost for software teams, so cutting it while keeping correctness is a relevant goal. The results are self-reported on the authors' own benchmark, and the theoretical claims rest on stated assumptions, so the gains should be checked by independent evaluation before weighing them heavily.

papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly produce AI slop in generated code: verbose, redundant, non-idiomatic implementations that pass functional checks but bloat codebases. The problem compounds on SDKs released after the model's training cutoff, where the model has neither idiomatic priors nor compositional understanding. We present Option-GRPO, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that adapts a code LLM to an unseen SDK from its source code alone, without human-written usage examples or test cases, and that explicitly optimizes for both functional correctness and code elegance. Our key insight is that SDK source code contains compositional structure that defines a hierarchy of reusable code patterns (code options) which simultaneously serve as the building blocks of a curriculum and the action space for efficient policy optimization. We show that code options induce a valid semi-Markov decision process, give conditional bounds under which shorter option description length implies more concise and, in expectation, more API-efficient programs, and analyze under stated assumptions how the option hierarchy improves credit assignment by a factor of $\sqrt{T/K}$. Using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with execution-based rewards at each curriculum level, Option-GRPO discovers SDK idioms, composes them into patterns, and assembles patterns into complete programs. Experiments on 12 unseen SDKs with a 32B-parameter base model demonstrate 61.4% pass@1, outperforming flat GRPO by 8.7 points, ExploraCoder by 11.2 points, and ReCode by 6.3 points. Option-GRPO produces solutions that use 34.7% fewer API calls and are 27% shorter than flat-GRPO outputs while maintaining higher correctness, directly attacking the slop problem.

papers.title: Towards Optimism-Pessimism Trade-off in Model-based Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22172v1

summary.background:
- Reinforcement learning (RL): an agent learns by trying actions and receiving rewards.
- Offline RL: learning only from a fixed dataset collected earlier, with no new interaction.
- Online fine-tuning: continuing to improve the learned policy through live interaction.
- Model-based RL: the agent learns a model of how the environment behaves and plans with it.
- Optimism vs. pessimism: optimism favors uncertain actions that might pay off; pessimism avoids them. Both are used to handle uncertainty from limited data.
- Pareto front: a set of solutions where improving one objective requires worsening another.
- Soft actor-critic: a common RL algorithm that rewards both task success and action randomness.
- Contextual bandit: a simple method for choosing among options based on observed context and feedback.
summary.one_liner: A model-based offline-to-online RL method that trains a Pareto pool of optimistic-to-pessimistic policies offline (via a multi-objective soft actor-critic, MOSAIC) and uses a hierarchical contextual bandit to pick among them during online fine-tuning (HiP3).
summary.plain: Robots and game-playing agents are often first trained on a fixed batch of past data and then keep learning while acting in the real setting. This paper addresses the problem that the switch from the old data to new experience can make learning worse. Instead of committing to one cautious-or-bold setting during the first stage, the authors train a set of policies spanning that trade-off and let the agent choose among them as it goes.
summary.why: The core idea is that the best level of caution depends on the new task, so deferring that choice to online fine-tuning may avoid costly tuning. The text reports the strongest aggregate performance across same and novel online tasks, but gives no further detail here, so the size and generality of the gain should be checked in the full paper. It may be of interest to people working on sample-efficient adaptation of learned controllers.

papers.abstract: Model-based offline-to-online reinforcement learning (RL) enables sample-efficient adaptation by leveraging offline pre-training for online fine-tuning. However, the distribution shifts between offline and online stages often hinder fine-tuning performance. Many existing methods encode the optimism-pessimism trade-off through a single-objective formulation. Selecting its trade-off coefficient through online fine-tuning can require costly bi-level optimization. We identify the balance established during offline training as a key challenge: in our motivating experiments, optimistic policies adapt better to novel tasks, whereas pessimistic policies perform better on the same online tasks. To address this challenge, we propose a bi-objective formulation that captures this trade-off, yielding a Pareto policy pool during offline training. This policy pool enables adaptive selection during online fine-tuning across diverse online tasks. To generate the pool, we introduce Multi-Objective Soft Actor-critIC (MOSAIC), which solves bi-objective problems and constructs diverse Pareto policies. After offline training, a contextual bandit algorithm hierarchically selects the most suitable policy for fine-tuning at each online interaction step. Empirically, our pipeline, Hierarchical Pareto Policy Pool (HiP3), achieves the strongest aggregate performance across both same and novel online tasks and maintains its advantage under stronger distribution shifts. Comprehensive ablations further clarify the roles of the policy pool, MOSAIC-based pool construction, and the online selection mechanism.

papers.title: Contrastive Activation-Guided Zeroth-Order Preference Optimisation for Memory-Efficient LLM Alignment
papers.label: arXiv:2611.20635v1

summary.background:
- Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF): training a model to prefer answers people rate highly.
- Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO): a simpler RLHF variant that learns directly from pairs of chosen and rejected responses.
- Backpropagation: the standard method for computing how to adjust each weight; it requires storing activations, which uses a lot of memory.
- Zeroth-order optimisation: estimating improvement by trying random small changes to the model and measuring the effect, with no gradient calculation.
- Isotropic perturbation: random nudges spread equally in all directions; the paper argues these are noisy for preference objectives.
- Low-rank subspace: a small set of directions that captures most of the useful variation, used here to focus the nudges.
- Activations: the intermediate values inside a neural network for a given input.
- Peak GPU memory and sequence length: how much graphics-card memory training needs at its maximum, and how long each input text is in tokens.
summary.one_liner: CA-ZODPO is a zeroth-order (backpropagation-free) preference-optimisation method for aligning LLMs that builds a low-rank search subspace from the activation difference between chosen and rejected responses, with momentum kept in that subspace.
summary.plain: Training large language models to match human preferences usually needs a lot of computer memory, because the standard training method stores intermediate results for every layer. This paper proposes a way to train with much less memory by estimating improvements from guessed nudges to the model rather than computing exact gradients, and by aiming those nudges at the directions where good and bad answers differ. On a 1.5-billion-parameter Qwen2.5 model and the Anthropic HH-RLHF dataset, the authors report it beats common zeroth-order baselines, stays competitive with standard first-order DPO in pairwise preference tests, and cuts peak GPU memory by about 59% at sequence length 2048.
summary.why: Reducing the memory cost of preference alignment could make fine-tuning feasible on smaller hardware, which matters for wider access to aligned models. The text reports results on a single model and dataset only, so how well the gains hold at other scales or tasks is not shown here.

papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO) simplifies reinforcement learning from human feedback, but still relies on traditional backpropagation and its associated activation-memory cost. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimisation avoids backpropagation, yet isotropic perturbations can produce noisy updates for preference objectives defined by differences between chosen and rejected responses. We introduce Contrastive Activation-guided Zeroth-Order Direct Preference Optimisation (CA-ZODPO), which constructs a low-rank search subspace from the activation discrepancy between the chosen and rejected responses in each preference pair. Perturbations are restricted to this subspace, while momentum is maintained in low-rank coordinates to preserve the memory advantages of ZO training. On Qwen2.5-1.5B with Anthropic HH-RLHF, CA-ZODPO outperforms common ZO baselines and remains competitive with first-order DPO in pairwise preference evaluation. It also reduces peak GPU memory by about 59\% at a sequence length of 2048 while retaining the sequence-length scaling behaviour of zeroth-order training.

papers.title: RIFT: Reward Improvement Field Transfer for Cross-Domain Offline RL
papers.label: arXiv:2611.19681v1

summary.background:
- Offline reinforcement learning: learning a control policy from a fixed log of past experience, with no new interaction.
- Transition: one step of experience (state, action, next state, reward).
- Dynamics shift: the same actions lead to different outcomes in a different environment (e.g., different gravity or friction).
- Optimal transport: a way of matching points between two sets with minimal total movement; here it pairs low- and high-reward transitions.
- Affine field: a simple linear map (scaling plus shifting) fitted to the displacements between paired points.
- Latent space: a compressed representation in which source and target data are encoded together.
- Data augmentation: creating extra synthetic training examples to enlarge a dataset.
summary.one_liner: RIFT transfers learned low-to-high reward improvement directions from abundant source-domain transitions to augment scarce target-domain offline RL data, using optimal-transport pairing and an affine displacement field in a shared latent space.
summary.plain: Robots and simulated agents often have little data from the environment they actually need to control, but plenty from a related environment with different physics. This paper proposes a way to borrow from that other environment: instead of copying its experiences directly, it learns how moving from poor outcomes to good outcomes looks in the source data, then applies that same kind of shift to poor examples in the target data to create new training examples. The authors report improved overall performance over existing baselines on locomotion tasks where gravity, body shape, or friction changes.
summary.why: Reusing data across differing environments is a practical bottleneck for offline learning, where an agent must learn from a fixed dataset without trying new actions. The paper's theoretical claims (an error bound, conditions for when target anchoring beats direct transplanting, and a link to downstream return) are the parts most worth checking, though the text gives only a summary of these results and does not show their details.

papers.abstract: Learning from limited target data is a central challenge in cross-domain offline reinforcement learning. Abundant source data can help, but dynamics differences can make direct transition reuse unreliable. We propose Reward Improvement Field Transfer (RIFT), which instead learns how low- and high-reward source transitions differ. RIFT encodes source and target transitions in a shared latent space, pairs low- and high-reward source transitions using optimal transport, and fits an affine field to their displacements. It applies this field to low-reward target anchors and decodes the results to augment the target dataset. The approach builds on the hypothesis that related domains can share useful low-to-high reward structure despite different dynamics. We bound synthesis error under shared class geometry, identify conditions favoring target anchoring over source-high transplant, and derive a conditional connection to downstream return. Experiments on dense-reward locomotion tasks under gravity, morphology, and friction shifts show improved aggregate performance over existing baselines.
